strengths: Clear problem identification: articulates a novel and well-motivated insight that existing image editing systems suffer from imbalanced division of responsibilities, with the generation module overburdened with design tasks

Substantial dataset contributions: DIM-T2I (14M images) and DIM-Edit (233K pairs) with thoughtful curation; demonstrates that real-world images with rich long-context annotations outperform filtered datasets

Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA/competitive performance on ImgEdit and GEdit-Bench-EN while being 10× smaller (generative params) than Step1X-Edit and UniWorld-V1; outperforms models with 7-14B parameters

Rigorous experimental validation: comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 7-8) isolating contributions of different data components and CoT elements; consistent evaluation methodology; robustness testing across different external designers

Reproducible and simple architecture: uses lightweight 2-layer MLP connector rather than complex designs, suggesting improvements stem from data quality; hyperparameters documented; promises to release datasets and models
Well-designed dataset creation pipeline: sophisticated DIM-Edit creation process with multi-stage quality assessment (misaligned/partially aligned/aligned) and structured 4-step CoT generation stages

Thorough evaluation across multiple benchmarks: GenEval, MJHQ-30K, ImgEdit, and GEdit-Bench-EN; visual comparisons clearly demonstrate advantages; fair baseline comparisons using consistent evaluation metric (GPT-4.1)
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: model requires external designer (GPT-4o) during inference to generate CoT blueprints; cannot operate independently, adding computational cost and raising questions about whether improvements come from better data organization or leveraging a more capable external model

Limited architectural and methodological novelty: model is straightforward combination of frozen MLLM + trainable DiT + simple connector; primary contribution is dataset-centric rather than algorithmic innovation

Inadequately addressed data leakage concerns: DIM-Edit is derived from existing datasets (UltraEdit, ShareGPT-4o-Image, MagicBrush, SEED-Data-Edit-Part3); while distillation datasets excluded, potential overlap with evaluation benchmarks not thoroughly investigated; Janus-4o comparison provides incomplete assurance

Unvalidated DIM-T2I annotation quality: 14M images annotated by in-house models across 21 dimensions without human evaluation; no verification of annotation quality, coverage, or inter-annotator agreement; claims about 'broad coverage' lack empirical support

Performance gaps not fully resolved: underperforms Step1X-Edit on GEdit-Bench-EN (6.18 vs. 6.44); shows significant weakness on text-change tasks (2.34 vs. 7.72) due to missing training data, representing a notable blind spot for general editing

Incomplete failure analysis: limited discussion of when/why approach fails; no analysis of boundary conditions, sensitivity to poor CoT quality, or degradation with weak external guidance; ablations show what helps but not why

Unaddressed generalization questions: unclear how model performs with inconsistent or poor-quality CoT from external designer; zero-shot or human-provided CoT capability not demonstrated; robustness to different reasoning quality unexplored
Insufficient architectural justification: limited explanation for why 2-layer MLP suffices or why freezing Qwen2.5-VL-3B is optimal; no ablations on connector design choices or sensitivity analysis

T2I evaluation limitations: DIM-T2I contribution somewhat disconnected from editing focus; GenEval uses LLM-rewritten prompts which may diminish the value of long-context annotations; no direct analysis of how 21-dimensional annotations benefit T2I
Missing reproducibility details: computational cost and training time not discussed; inference latency with GPT-4o dependency not analyzed; details of 'in-house models' used for annotation vague

strengths: Clear and well-articulated motivation addressing imbalanced responsibility division in image editing models
Strong empirical results on ImgEdit and GEdit-Bench-EN benchmarks with compact model size
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 7-8) demonstrating the contribution of dataset components and CoT elements
Practical dataset creation pipeline with multi-stage quality assessment and optimization
Demonstration of generalizability across different designer models (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL-3B)
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair experimental comparison: DIM uses external GPT-4o designer at inference while baselines do not, making the performance comparison asymmetric and potentially misleading
Heavy dependency on proprietary GPT-4o model at inference creates reproducibility issues, costly deployment, and limits practical applicability
Limited technical novelty: architecture is straightforward combination of frozen MLLM + trainable DiT + simple 2-layer MLP connector, similar to prior work (MetaQuery)
Potential data contamination: DIM-Edit contains 46K samples from ShareGPT-4o-Image, which may overlap with GEdit-Bench evaluation sources; no truly held-out test evaluation provided
Weak performance on Text Change task in GEdit-Bench-EN (2.34 vs 7.40 for Step1X-Edit) suggests significant limitations not adequately discussed
Marginal improvements on T2I benchmarks (nearly identical to MetaQuery-L) question the value of the 14M DIM-T2I dataset
Missing critical evaluations: no human evaluation, no sensitivity analysis for designer quality, no error analysis or failure case discussion
Computational cost of GPT-4o inference during editing not discussed despite being a significant practical limitation
When using Qwen2.5-VL-3B designer instead of GPT-4o (DIM-4.6B-Edit-Q3B), performance drops to 3.49, worse than Step1X-Edit's 3.06, suggesting the improvement heavily depends on GPT-4o's capabilities
Visual comparisons (Figure 3) are cherry-picked examples without systematic evaluation methodology

strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight about imbalanced responsibilities in image editing—identifying that the understanding module should handle design while the generation module focuses on painting is compelling and grounded in human workflows
Strong empirical results on ImgEdit benchmark (3.67 vs 3.06 for Step1X-Edit) despite having 10× fewer generative parameters, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed data-centric approach

High-quality dataset contributions: DIM-T2I with 14M images annotated across 21 dimensions yielding 146.76 average prompt length (far exceeding existing datasets), and DIM-Edit with thoughtfully curated 233K editing pairs including multi-stage quality filtering

Thorough and rigorous experimental validation including comprehensive ablations (Tables 7-8), multi-benchmark evaluation, clear visualization of improvements, and robustness testing with different external designers
Elegant architectural simplicity (2-layer MLP connector) that makes the data-driven nature of improvements unambiguous and avoids confounds from architectural innovation

Clear dataset creation pipeline with well-documented rationale—the distinction between misaligned/partially-aligned/aligned prompts and appropriate remediation strategies demonstrates careful engineering
weaknesses: Critical structural dependency on GPT-4o for both training and inference creates circular dependency where the model learns to mimic GPT-4o's reasoning style rather than developing generalizable design understanding; outsources design responsibility to proprietary external model rather than learning it end-to-end

Overclaimed SOTA status: on GEdit-Bench-EN full set (6.18 vs 6.44 for Step1X-Edit), the model actually underperforms; claims should be more precise given strong performance on only subset of benchmarks and severe weakness on Text Change task (2.34 vs 7.72)

Limited generalization analysis: no evaluation on editing specifications from humans or other AI models; unclear how robust the model is to different annotation styles beyond GPT-4o-generated specifications, raising concerns about overfitting to GPT-4o's reasoning patterns

Reproducibility limitations: 14M web-crawled images with 21-dimension in-house annotation is difficult for others to replicate; practical access to released dataset may be restricted; exact methodology for in-house model annotations is unclear

Potential data contamination: DIM-Edit includes 46K samples from ShareGPT-4o-Image which was also used in Janus-4o training, making the baseline comparison less clear-cut; quality filtering entirely depends on GPT-4o judgments which could introduce systematic biases

Incomplete analysis of T2I contribution: marginal improvement over MetaQuery on GenEval (0.77 vs 0.78) is within noise; unclear how much editing performance gains come from DIM-T2I vs. editing-specific DIM-Edit; missing targeted ablation to isolate T2I's impact

Limited evaluation methodology: uses only GPT-4.1 for evaluation without human validation; no human evaluation studies to verify that GPT-based metrics align with human perception; no analysis of failure modes beyond brief mention of Text Change task weakness
Significant computational cost not discussed: using GPT-4o at inference time has API costs and latency implications that limit practical deployment; no analysis provided of this overhead
Missing design ablations: 21 annotation dimensions and 4-step CoT structure appear somewhat arbitrary; no sensitivity analysis on prompt length, number of dimensions, or CoT structure choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clear articulation of imbalanced responsibilities between understanding and generation modules with intuitive human workflow analogy
Strong empirical results: Achieves SOTA on ImgEdit (3.67), near-SOTA on GEdit-Bench (6.18 excluding text task), with 4.5× inference speedup over larger competitors despite using only 4.6B params
Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablations (data composition, CoT components, initialization), multiple benchmarks, honest failure case disclosure, and self-play evaluation

High-quality dataset contributions: DIM-T2I with 21 thoughtfully-designed dimensions (14M pairs, 146.76 avg words); DIM-Edit with 83.4% ultra-high quality and 89% human preference over raw instructions
Robust generalization: Demonstrates compatibility with multiple external designers (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3.5-8B, GLM-4.1V-9B) showing approach is not model-specific
Strong reproducibility effort: Detailed data collection pipelines, quality assessment methodology, dimension specifications, and commitment to release dataset and models
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Intentionally minimalist architecture (frozen MLLM + 2-layer MLP + trainable DiT) provides little methodological contribution; innovation is primarily data-centric rather than algorithmic

Inference design contradicts unified model claims: Requires external designer model at inference to generate CoT blueprints, adding computational overhead and external dependency; self-play variant (3.49) significantly underperforms main model (3.67)

Dataset reproducibility concerns: DIM-T2I relies on unspecified 'in-house models' with no detailed description; DIM-Edit entirely dependent on GPT-4o creating reproducibility barrier; dataset creation costs not discussed

Significant capability gaps: Text Change task performs 76% worse than Step1X-Edit (2.99 vs 7.40); acknowledged failures in complex text rendering, geometric shapes, and reference-free editing substantially limit practical applicability

Evaluation limitations: ImgEdit/GEdit-Bench-EN evaluation uses GPT-4 scoring potentially introducing bias; performance margins sometimes modest (12.6% improvement on ImgEdit); different experimental conditions across comparisons (VAE compression, proprietary data)

Insufficient CoT analysis: Limited investigation of why/what CoT captures beyond empirical validation; claim that CoT 'removes design responsibility' oversimplified since generation module still executes complex plans; no analysis of CoT quality distribution across task types

strengths: Clear and intuitive problem articulation with the designer-painter roles concept
Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on ImgEdit (3.67 vs 3.26) with 5× fewer parameters than competitors
Valuable dataset contributions: 14M DIM-T2I pairs with comprehensive 21-dimensional annotations and 233K high-quality DIM-Edit CoT annotations (83.4% ultra-high quality)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple benchmarks, extensive ablations (Tables 8-9), and generalization studies across external designers
Thorough reproducibility details with promised dataset/model release and honest discussion of failure cases
4.5× inference speedup compared to Step1X-Edit with maintained editing quality
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: 2-layer MLP architecture lacks innovation; approach is essentially standard CoT prompting well-established in prior work
Core claim about designer-painter imbalance is intuitive but not rigorously validated—improvements may simply stem from longer prompts (DIM-T2I) rather than conceptual rebalancing
Critical dependency on external GPT-4o for best results: internal designer (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) achieves only 3.49 vs 3.67 with GPT-4o, contradicting claim that model internalizes design responsibility
Insufficient ablation of confounded factors: cannot cleanly isolate contributions of longer-context prompts alone, CoT structure, and frozen MLLM design
Dataset constructed entirely on GPT-4o-generated CoT annotations—model may simply imitate GPT-4o's reasoning style rather than learn true planning; no human CoT annotations
Moderate empirical improvements (12.6% on ImgEdit); GEdit-Bench-EN performance essentially tied with Step1X-Edit excluding text task, where Step1X excels (7.40 vs 2.99)
Oversold conceptual framing: title emphasizes 'rebalancing roles' but actual implementation is 'use external GPT-4o prompts'; frozen MLLM is never truly assigned design responsibility
Missing critical ablations: no analysis of what frozen MLLM contributes vs trainable DiT; why 2-layer MLP suffices compared to MetaQuery's 1.6B connector; comparison with longer-prompt-only baseline
No statistical significance testing with error bars despite competitive baseline numbers; single-run results reported
Practical applicability limited by requiring GPT-4o access for best performance; internal-only capability (3.49) underperforms existing models

strengths: Novel problem formulation identifying imbalanced responsibility between understanding and generation modules in unified image editing models
Rigorous and comprehensive dataset construction with 14M T2I samples across 21 dimensions and 233K CoT-annotated editing samples; high quality validation (83.4% ultra-high quality)
Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA or competitive performance on ImgEdit and GEdit-Bench while being 5× smaller (4.6B vs 12.5B parameters) with 4.5× faster inference
Thorough experimental evaluation with multiple benchmarks, comprehensive ablations on data composition, CoT components, and initialization strategies
Demonstrates generalizability across different external designers (Table 6) and effectiveness of self-play configuration (Table 7)
Practical efficiency with simple architecture (2-layer MLP connector) achieving superior results
High reproducibility with detailed methods, promised public release of resources, and extensive appendices documenting data pipeline and quality assessment
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: model design is straightforward (frozen MLLM + trainable DiT + 2-layer MLP); contribution is primarily dataset-driven rather than methodological
Dependency on external designer (GPT-4o) for optimal inference performance reduces practical applicability; unclear whether approach generalizes to cheaper/open-source designers consistently

ShareGPT-4o-Image data included in DIM-Edit while comparing against Janus-4o trained on same data raises potential evaluation bias concerns
